title: Healthiest Alcohol to Drink: Best and Worst Choices, Ranked
excerpt: Is any alcohol actually healthy? An honest look at the least harmful liquor, beer, and wine by sugar, calories, and congeners, and why the amount matters more than the drink.
metaDescription: What's the healthiest alcohol to drink? Honest rankings of liquor, beer, and wine by sugar, calories, and congeners, plus why no drink is truly healthy.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no truly healthy alcohol. Every alcoholic drink delivers the same main ingredient, ethanol, and ethanol is what raises cancer risk, strains the liver, disrupts sleep, and adds empty calories. What differs between drinks is everything *around* the ethanol: how much of it you get per glass, how much sugar and how many calories ride along, and how many by-products (called congeners) come with it. If you're going to drink, the "healthiest" choices are the ones that make it easy to drink less ethanol, with little sugar and few extras: a spirit like vodka, gin, or blanco tequila with soda water and citrus, a dry wine in a measured 5 oz pour, a light beer, or a plain hard seltzer.

**The quick picks:**

- **Lowest sugar and calories:** a 1.5 oz shot of clear spirit with soda water and lime (about 100 calories, close to zero sugar).
- **Easiest to pace:** light beer or a plain hard seltzer (about 100 calories and roughly 4-5% alcohol, so a can lasts).
- **Best wine pick:** a dry red or dry white in a true 5 oz pour, not a 9 oz restaurant glass.
- **Fewest hangover-linked extras:** clear spirits like vodka and gin, which carry far fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, or dark rum.
- **What to avoid:** sugary cocktails and premade mixes, "big" craft beers above 8% alcohol, and large wine pours, because they quietly double your ethanol or sugar intake.

> **A quick health note.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Talk to your doctor before drinking at all if** you're pregnant or trying to conceive, take prescription medicine (many common drugs interact with alcohol), have liver disease, pancreatitis, heart rhythm problems, or a personal or strong family history of cancer, or have been told to limit alcohol. **Get urgent care** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning; call 911 in the US.

## Why "Healthiest Alcohol" Is a Bit of a Trick Question

For years, people heard that a glass of red wine a day was good for the heart. That idea came mostly from observational studies, where researchers compare people who already drink moderately with people who don't. Those studies kept finding that light drinkers seemed healthier than non-drinkers, and the result got turned into a health tip.

The problem is who ends up in the "non-drinker" group. It often includes people who quit because they were already sick, people with a history of heavy drinking, and people who avoid alcohol for health reasons. Researchers call this the "sick quitter" problem. Light drinkers also tend to be wealthier, more active, and better fed. When newer analyses separated lifetime non-drinkers from former drinkers and controlled for these differences, most of the apparent benefit faded. A large 2023 meta-analysis in *JAMA Network Open*, pooling more than 100 cohort studies, found that low-volume drinking was not linked to a lower risk of death from any cause compared with lifetime non-drinking.

Official guidance has moved in the same direction:

- **The World Health Organization** stated in 2023 that no level of alcohol consumption can be considered safe for health, mainly because of cancer risk.
- **The International Agency for Research on Cancer** classifies alcoholic drinks as a Group 1 carcinogen, the same category as tobacco smoke. It's linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, colon and rectum, and breast.
- **The US Surgeon General** issued an advisory in early 2025 on alcohol and cancer risk, calling for clearer warnings on labels.
- **Canada's 2023 Guidance on Alcohol and Health** places the low-risk zone at about two standard drinks a week or fewer.
- **The Dietary Guidelines for Americans** say that adults who choose to drink should limit themselves to 2 drinks or fewer a day for men and 1 or fewer for women, and that drinking less is better for health than drinking more.

None of this means one drink with dinner is dangerous. Risk rises with the dose, and at low intake the extra risk is small. It just means that the useful question isn't "which alcohol is good for me?" It's "if I'm going to drink, which choices keep the downside smallest?" That question has real answers.

## What Actually Makes One Drink "Less Bad" Than Another

Five things separate a better choice from a worse one. In order of importance:

### 1. How much ethanol you actually get

This matters far more than anything else on this list. Your liver doesn't care whether ethanol came from a fine Burgundy or a can of beer; it processes it the same way. A US standard drink is 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is about:

- 12 oz of regular beer at 5% alcohol
- 5 oz of wine at 12%
- 1.5 oz of 80-proof (40%) spirits

The trap is that real servings rarely match these. A 16 oz pint of a 7% IPA is close to two standard drinks. A generous restaurant wine pour of 8 or 9 oz at 14% is close to two and a half. A strong mixed drink with two or three pours of liquor can be three. If you want a quick reference for common drinks, our [alcohol content by drink guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) lays out the numbers.

So the healthiest drink is usually the one that makes it hardest to overdo it: lower in alcohol, served in a measured amount, and slow to finish.

### 2. Sugar

Many drinks carry a lot of sugar on top of the alcohol. Regular soda mixers, premade margarita and daiquiri mixes, sweet liqueurs, dessert wines, and many flavored malt drinks can add several teaspoons of sugar per serving. A 12 oz can of regular cola alone has close to 40 grams. Sugar adds calories, spikes blood sugar, and makes drinks easier to gulp, which brings you back to problem number one.

### 3. Calories

Alcohol itself has about 7 calories per gram, nearly as much as fat. That means one standard drink carries roughly 100 calories from the ethanol alone before any mixer or residual sugar. Those calories don't fill you up, and alcohol tends to increase appetite. For more on this, see our guides on [the lowest-calorie alcohol](/never-hungover/lowest-calorie-alcohol) and [why alcohol makes you hungry](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-hungry).

### 4. Congeners

Congeners are by-products of fermentation and aging, things like methanol, acetaldehyde, other alcohols, and the compounds that give whiskey and brandy their color and flavor. Dark spirits generally carry more of them than clear spirits. In a well-known 2010 study in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, Rohsenow and colleagues gave volunteers either bourbon or vodka to the same blood alcohol level. The bourbon group reported worse hangovers, though next-day performance was similar. Congeners don't change your long-term health risk much compared with the ethanol itself, but they do seem to make mornings worse. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper.

### 5. Other additives and sensitivities

Some people react to things that ride along in specific drinks: histamines and tannins in red wine, sulfites in wine (a real but less common trigger), gluten in beer for people with celiac disease, or artificial sweeteners in "zero sugar" mixers. These matter a lot for some people and not at all for others.

## The Healthiest Alcohol Options, Ranked

Here's how the main categories compare, assuming a standard serving. Calorie figures are typical ranges, and specific brands vary.

| Drink (standard serving) | Typical calories | Sugar | Congeners | Main thing to watch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vodka, gin, or blanco tequila + soda water and citrus (1.5 oz) | about 100 | near zero | low | Easy to drink fast; pours creep up |
| Plain hard seltzer (12 oz, ~5%) | about 100 | 0-2 g | low | Flavored or "extra" versions have more alcohol |
| Light beer (12 oz, ~4%) | about 95-110 | low | moderate | Volume adds up quickly |
| Dry red or dry white wine (5 oz) | about 120-125 | 1-2 g or less | moderate (red higher) | Large pours, higher-alcohol wines |
| Brut or extra brut sparkling wine (5 oz) | about 110-120 | low | moderate | Bubbles may speed absorption |
| Neat whiskey or aged rum (1.5 oz) | about 100 | near zero | high | Rougher hangovers for many people |
| Regular beer (12 oz, ~5%) | about 150 | low | moderate | Fine in moderation; easy to have several |
| Craft IPA or stout (12-16 oz, 6-10%) | about 200-350 | varies | moderate-high | Often 1.5-2.5 standard drinks per glass |
| Cocktails with juice, syrup, or premade mix | about 200-500 | high | varies | Sugar plus multiple pours |
| Dessert wine or sweet liqueur (small pour) | varies | high | varies | Concentrated sugar |

The pattern is simple. The top of the list has one measured pour of alcohol and almost nothing else. The bottom of the list has more alcohol than it looks, more sugar, or both.

## What Is the Healthiest Liquor?

If you're choosing a spirit, **clear, unflavored spirits like vodka, gin, and 100% agave blanco tequila** are the best picks. They have almost no sugar or carbohydrates when taken neat or with soda water, and they're lower in congeners than darker spirits.

A few common claims deserve a closer look:

- **"Tequila is healthy because of agave."** The agave plant contains fibers called agavins that have been studied for possible metabolic effects, but the distillation process doesn't leave meaningful amounts of them in the finished spirit. Tequila is a reasonable choice because a 100% agave blanco is clean and low in congeners, not because it's a health food. Look for "100% agave" on the label; cheaper "mixto" tequilas can include other sugars. Our [tequila hangover guide](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) covers the myths.
- **"Vodka is the cleanest drink."** Vodka has the fewest congeners of the common spirits, which may help with hangovers. It's still pure ethanol, and because it's so neutral, it's easy to drink a lot without noticing.
- **"Whiskey is healthier because it has antioxidants."** Aged spirits do pick up compounds from the barrel, some with antioxidant activity in a lab dish. There's no good evidence that these amounts do anything meaningful for your health, and the congeners that come along with them are linked to worse hangovers.

All 80-proof spirits have about the same calories per shot, roughly 95-100. Higher-proof bottles have more. Flavored vodkas and "spiced" rums may add sugar.

**The mixer matters more than the spirit.** A vodka soda and a vodka cranberry contain the same vodka, but the cranberry version can carry 20-30 grams of sugar. The best mixers are soda water, sparkling mineral water, fresh lime or lemon, a splash of real juice, or a light tonic. Regular tonic water is sweeter than people expect, often close to a soda.

## What Is the Healthiest Beer?

The healthiest beers are **light lagers and session beers** around 4% alcohol or lower. They have fewer calories, fewer carbohydrates, and less ethanol per can than a regular beer, and much less than a craft IPA.

Some things to know about beer:

- **Alcohol content is the main driver of calories in beer.** A 4% light beer is usually around 100 calories per 12 oz. A 5% regular beer is around 150. A 9% double IPA can be over 250 in the same 12 oz, and many are served in 16 oz cans or pints.
- **"Low-carb" doesn't mean low-alcohol.** Some low-carb beers are full strength. Check the percentage.
- **Non-alcoholic beer is the genuinely healthier beer.** Modern non-alcoholic beers under 0.5% alcohol give you the taste and ritual with very little ethanol. If you're curious how little is in them, see our article on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol).
- **Gluten-free options exist.** People with celiac disease need beer made from gluten-free grains, or should check with their doctor about "gluten-reduced" beers, which are made from barley and treated to break down gluten.

Beer also tends to be drunk in volume, which is why the "beer hangover" is so common. Our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) covers why.

## What Is the Healthiest Wine? (And Is Red Wine Actually Good for You?)

The healthiest wines are **dry wines with moderate alcohol**, around 11-13%, served in an honest 5 oz pour. Dry reds and dry whites typically have only a gram or two of sugar per glass. Brut and extra brut sparkling wines are also low in sugar. Sweet wines like moscato, late-harvest whites, port, and other dessert wines have much more.

**About red wine and the heart.** Red wine contains polyphenols, including resveratrol, which have shown interesting effects in lab and animal studies. But the amount of resveratrol in a glass of wine is small, far below the doses used in most of that research, and human studies of resveratrol supplements have been mixed at best. The "red wine is heart-healthy" claim rests mostly on the same observational studies that newer, better-controlled analyses have undercut. Major heart organizations, including the American Heart Association, do not recommend that non-drinkers start drinking wine for heart health. If you want the polyphenols, grapes, berries, and other plant foods supply them without the ethanol.

**Red vs white.** Red wine has more polyphenols and more congeners, plus more histamine and tannins. Some people get headaches from red wine that they don't get from white. Our [red wine headache guide](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) explains the possible causes, and our article on [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) explains why sulfites are usually not the culprit people assume.

**"Clean," organic, and natural wines.** These labels describe farming and winemaking choices. They may mean fewer added sulfites or no added sugar, and some people prefer them for those reasons. They're still wine, with the same ethanol, and there is no good evidence that they're meaningfully healthier or that they prevent hangovers. A lower-alcohol "clean" wine is better than a higher-alcohol one mainly because it has less alcohol.

**Watch the pour.** A standard 5 oz glass of 12% wine is one drink. A 9 oz glass of 14.5% Zinfandel is more than two. Pour size is the biggest wine variable that people overlook.

## What Is the Healthiest Alcohol for Your Liver?

There isn't one. Your liver breaks down ethanol the same way no matter what drink it came in, first into acetaldehyde (a toxic compound) and then into acetate. The damage that leads to fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, and cirrhosis tracks with **how much ethanol you drink and how often**, not with the type of drink.

What helps the liver is:

- **Fewer total drinks per week.** This matters more than anything else.
- **Alcohol-free days.** Many liver specialists suggest several alcohol-free days a week so the liver isn't processing alcohol every day.
- **Avoiding binges.** Large amounts at once hit the liver harder than the same total spread out, and binges carry their own risks.
- **Not combining alcohol with liver-heavy medicines** like high doses of acetaminophen. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for why that matters.
- **Lower sugar.** Fructose from sugary mixers is also processed in the liver, and high sugar intake is linked to fatty liver on its own. A sugary cocktail adds a second load.

If you drink regularly and have been told your liver enzymes are high, or you have fatty liver disease, talk to your doctor about whether any amount of alcohol is right for you.

## What Is the Healthiest Alcohol for Weight Loss or Low-Sugar Diets?

If you're watching calories, carbohydrates, or blood sugar, the best options are:

1. **Clear spirits with soda water and citrus**, about 100 calories and close to zero carbs.
2. **Plain hard seltzer**, about 100 calories and 0-2 grams of sugar per 12 oz.
3. **Light beer**, about 100 calories and 3-6 grams of carbs.
4. **Dry wine or brut sparkling wine**, about 120 calories per 5 oz with very little sugar.

Two cautions:

- **Alcohol slows fat burning while your body processes it.** Your body prioritizes clearing ethanol, so it puts other fuel use on hold. That's one reason even "low-calorie" drinks don't fit neatly into a weight-loss plan. Our [alcohol and weight loss guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) has more.
- **People with diabetes face a low blood sugar risk.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar for hours after drinking, especially in people taking insulin or certain diabetes pills, and the symptoms can look like being drunk. Eat when you drink and talk to your doctor about a plan. Our [alcohol and diabetes guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) explains more.

If you're on a ketogenic diet, the same low-sugar choices apply, and many people find their tolerance drops noticeably. See our [alcohol and keto guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025).

## Healthiest Alcohol for Fewer Hangovers

Health and hangovers overlap but aren't the same thing. A drink can be "healthier" in terms of calories and still give you a rough morning if you drink it fast.

For fewer hangovers, the evidence-backed factors are:

- **Less total alcohol.** Hangover severity rises with how much you drink.
- **Fewer congeners.** Clear spirits and lighter drinks tend to produce milder hangovers than dark spirits for the same amount of alcohol.
- **Slower drinking with food.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Water between drinks.** Alcohol increases urination, and dehydration adds to the headache and thirst.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, which is a big part of why you feel bad the next day.

We ranked the common drinks by hangover potential in our [least hangover alcohol guide](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked). The short answer there lines up with this page: clear spirits, light beer, and dry white wine sit near the top; dark spirits, red wine, and sugary cocktails sit near the bottom. And mixing drinks matters less than the total amount, which is why the old "beer before liquor" rule doesn't hold up (see our [beer before liquor myth piece](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth)).

## The Healthiest Way to Drink (This Matters More Than the Drink)

If you only change one thing, change how much and how fast. These habits do more for your health than switching from whiskey to vodka:

- **Know your pours.** Use a jigger for spirits and a measured 5 oz pour for wine at home. It's eye-opening how much bigger free pours are.
- **Pick lower-strength versions.** A 4% beer instead of a 7% one, or an 11.5% wine instead of a 14.5% one, cuts your alcohol by a third or more with no extra effort.
- **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** One alcohol-free drink between each alcoholic one slows your pace and helps hydration.
- **Eat first and while drinking.** A meal with protein, fat, and fiber slows absorption.
- **Set a number before you start.** Deciding on two drinks before you go out works better than deciding in the moment.
- **Keep alcohol-free days.** Plenty of guidelines suggest several each week.
- **Don't drink to sleep.** Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster but breaks up the second half of the night.
- **Never mix with sedatives or opioids**, and check any prescription medicine with a pharmacist.

And the honest point: the healthiest option of all is a good non-alcoholic drink. Non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-free spirits, and sparkling drinks have improved a lot, and swapping in one or two per night is the single biggest upgrade you can make.

## Who Shouldn't Drink at All

For some people, there's no "healthiest" alcohol because the right amount is zero. That includes people who:

- Are pregnant or trying to get pregnant
- Are under the legal drinking age
- Take medicines that interact with alcohol, such as sedatives, some antidepressants, opioids, certain antibiotics, and blood thinners
- Have liver disease, pancreatitis, or certain heart rhythm problems
- Have been advised by a doctor not to drink
- Are planning to drive or operate machinery

If you're unsure whether alcohol fits with your health or your medications, a short conversation with your doctor or pharmacist is the best next step.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people who drink socially add a supplement to make the next morning easier. The most-studied option on this site is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal and lab studies suggest it may support the body's processing of alcohol and protect liver cells, and there's a small amount of human research, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising but not proven. There is no good evidence that DHM makes any alcohol "healthy," lowers cancer risk, or offsets heavy drinking.

If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter most. Treat any supplement as a small extra on top of drinking less, never a substitute for it.

## The Bottom Line

- No alcoholic drink is healthy. Ethanol is the main source of harm, and every drink contains it.
- The "healthiest" choices are the ones with less ethanol per serving, little or no sugar, and few congeners: clear spirits with soda water, plain hard seltzer, light beer, and dry wine in a 5 oz pour.
- For your liver and your long-term health, the amount you drink matters far more than the type.
- Red wine's heart benefits have largely not held up in better-designed research. Don't start drinking for your health.
- Measured pours, lower-strength drinks, food, water, and alcohol-free days do more good than any drink swap.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the healthiest alcohol to drink?**

No alcohol is truly healthy, but the least harmful choices are a clear spirit like vodka, gin, or 100% agave blanco tequila with soda water and citrus, a plain hard seltzer, a light beer, or a dry wine in a 5 oz pour. These keep sugar and calories low and make it easier to control how much alcohol you're drinking. The amount you drink matters much more than which of these you pick.

**What is the healthiest liquor?**

Clear, unflavored spirits like vodka, gin, and 100% agave blanco tequila are the best liquor choices. They have almost no sugar when served with soda water, and they carry fewer congeners than dark spirits like whiskey, brandy, and aged rum. All 80-proof spirits have about the same calories per shot, so the mixer usually makes the bigger difference.

**Is red wine actually good for your heart?**

The evidence is much weaker than it once seemed. Early observational studies suggested a benefit, but they often compared light drinkers with people who had quit drinking because of illness. Better-controlled analyses have found little or no benefit from light drinking. Red wine does contain polyphenols like resveratrol, but in small amounts. Heart organizations don't recommend starting to drink for heart health.

**What is the healthiest alcohol for your liver?**

There isn't one. Your liver processes ethanol the same way regardless of the drink, so liver harm depends on how much and how often you drink. Fewer drinks per week, regular alcohol-free days, avoiding binges, and skipping sugary mixers are what actually protect the liver. If you have liver disease or high liver enzymes, ask your doctor whether you should drink at all.

**What alcohol has the least sugar?**

Straight spirits like vodka, gin, tequila, and whiskey have essentially no sugar. Plain hard seltzers usually have 0-2 grams, dry wines a gram or two per glass, and brut sparkling wines are also low. Sugar mostly comes from mixers, liqueurs, premade cocktail mixes, sweet wines, and flavored malt drinks.

**Is vodka healthier than whiskey?**

Not in any meaningful long-term way, since both are mostly ethanol and have similar calories per shot. Vodka does have far fewer congeners, and research comparing vodka with bourbon found that bourbon produced worse hangovers at the same blood alcohol level. So vodka may be easier on your next morning, but it isn't better for your liver or your cancer risk.

**Is beer or wine healthier?**

Per standard drink, they're similar: a 12 oz 5% beer and a 5 oz glass of 12% wine contain about the same alcohol. Light beer is lower in calories than wine, and dry wine is lower in carbohydrates than regular beer. The bigger risk with both is serving size: craft beers and large wine pours often contain two or more standard drinks.

**Is hard seltzer healthier than beer?**

A plain hard seltzer is usually lower in calories and carbs than a regular beer and similar to a light beer, with about the same alcohol as a 5% beer. That makes it a reasonable pick if you're watching sugar or calories. Watch for "extra" or high-alcohol versions, which can contain 8% alcohol or more, and remember that the alcohol itself is the main health concern either way.
